howDoI.q: How do I see what a long sound costs on a slow computer?
How do I play a sound when the hero steps on something?
How do I put a crowd of monsters in a level, and what does it cost?
How do I animate a whole sky, and what does it cost?
Why does Escape restart the level?

pages.head: Welcome
pages.html:
Welcome

Slow Computers is a Starter: a small game that shows a few Game-Maker ideas, with signs in the levels that say what you are looking at. It has three short levels, and nothing in it can cost a life.

Play it first. Then open it in Game-Maker (Edit a copy on the home page keeps the original safe) and read the pages below.

The keys

Left and Right walk. Space jumps. F2 shows your lives, hit points and score.

Why this game is here

A game in 1994 had to run on whatever PC it met. The same game could be smooth on a fast machine and choppy on a slow one. A DOS game cannot change its computer, so the web player does it from outside: the Run like a menu in the corner of the player runs the game as a 286, a 386, a 486 or Today (the normal setting). Try each room on 286 first, then on the faster ones, and see what changes.

If your player has no speed setting, the game still plays and shows the same rooms at full speed.

pages.head: Level 1: Short and Long
pages.html:
Level 1: Short and Long

Eight pads lie along the ground: four short ones and four long ones. Each pad plays its sound once when you step on it. The short pads play a quarter-second blip. The long pads play a five-and-a-half-second run of bells. The music plays all the while.

Set the player to 286 and step on a short pad, then a long one. The long one freezes the game: you stop, the monsters stop, and then everything goes on. The music does not stop. On a 486 the same pad barely pauses the game, and on Today it does not pause it at all. There are four of each pad so you can try one at every speed.

pages.head: How this level is made
pages.html:
How this level is made

The pads are background blocks. A block can add to the score or to a counter when you touch it, and Game-Maker plays a sound for each of those changes. A block cannot name a sound itself, so the short pad adds 1 to the score, which plays the score sound (slot 5), and the long pad adds 1 to the money counter, which plays the coin sound (slot 2). In slowpc.snd those two slots have a digital sound: BLIP.VOC and LONGSND.VOC. Every other sound is a PC speaker blip.

When a block is touched it can turn into another block (its touch block). Here the touched cell turns into a pressed pad that does nothing, so one step plays one sound. A block that has an animation timer would not work for this: the timer changes every block of that kind at once, and it does not count from your touch.

The hero's money counter must be a real counter for the coin sound to play, so the game's character has money set to 1. A counter set to unlimited never changes and plays no sound.

Why does Escape restart the level?

Escape first ends the scene, then the screen fades to black. The game checks Escape again after the fade: it quits only if the key is still held. If you tap Escape and release it during the fade, the level can restart instead. On a slow computer, hold Escape until the screen goes black, then release it. The web player keeps this original DOS behavior.

pages.head: Level 2: A Crowd
pages.html:
Level 2: A Crowd

Thirty-six friendly monsters share one screen: ten gumdrops on the grass, eight snails in a lit cave below it and eighteen bees in two low rows. The cave is a cutaway: its solid grass roof carries you safely over the snails. They are all harmless: you walk through them.

Walk into the middle of the crowd on 286 and watch yourself. Your walking slows down, and so does the bees' flapping and the snails' creep, because the game could not finish a round of moving and drawing 36 monsters in time. On a 386 you will see a little less; on a 486 and Today nothing changes.

pages.head: How this level is made
pages.html:
How this level is made

The crowd is placed in the Map editor: every monster is a cell with a monster number. The kit's three monsters are in slowpc.mon: a gumdrop that paces back and forth, a bee that bobs up and down and a snail that creeps. Their power is 150, so you pass through them, and their picture blocks take no hit points.

The game draws at most 50 monsters on a screen, and only the ones that are on screen cost any time. Monsters off to the side do not slow the game until they scroll in. See Meet the Monsters for how a monster's path and power work.

pages.head: Level 3: Busy Sky
pages.html:
Level 3: Busy Sky

The whole sky is one animated block: a few pale wisps that drift a little every tick. Because every cell of the sky changes on every tick, the game has to draw each one again, again and again. On 286 a screenful of them takes a good part of every round, and the game slows a little. On a 486 and Today it does not.

pages.head: How this level is made
pages.html:
How this level is made

The sky block has a next block and a time of 1 tick. Eight blocks in a ring, each with the wisps a step further along, make the drift. A block's timer changes every cell of its kind at once, so one ring animates the whole sky. The wisps are only a step lighter than the sky, so the change is gentle, not a flash (see Flash Safe).

The same ring on only a few cells would cost very little. What costs is how many cells change on one tick.

pages.head: The numbers (estimates)
pages.html:
The numbers (estimates)

Game-Maker's clock ticks 18.2 times a second: one game tick is 54.9 milliseconds. Everything that moves runs once per tick. When a tick's work takes longer than that, the game does not catch up: it skips the tick it missed, so walking and animation get slower, while block timers and monster lifetimes (which count against the clock) stay exact.

The player's Run like a menu charges each tick the cost of the old machine. All of these are estimates worked out from period hardware figures, not measurements of a real PC, and the exact result depends on a real machine's video card and disk.

286 (12 MHz)386 (33 MHz)486 (66 MHz)IBM PS/1 Model 2011 (286, 10 MHz, 1 MB)
A quiet tick (the hero, the screen copy)20 ms9 ms4 ms24 ms
Each monster on screen1.8 ms0.8 ms0.35 ms2.2 ms
Each moving block redrawn0.25 ms0.12 ms0.05 ms0.3 ms
Reading a sound file from the disk30 ms, then about 400 bytes a millisecond18 ms, then about 80012 ms, then about 150080 ms, then about 150
Loading a level between levels (estimate: this game's 9 files, 158 KB)about 0.67 sabout 0.36 sabout 0.21 sabout 1.8 s
The music while a sound is readstops for the whole read, then goes on from where it was

So a 60 KB sound takes about 180 ms to read on a 286: three whole ticks. On a 486 it takes about 50 ms. On the IBM PS/1 (a 10 MHz 286 with 1 MB and a small, slow hard disk, no disk cache) it takes about 480 ms: nine ticks, and even the quarter-second blip takes about 100 ms. About twenty monsters fill a whole tick on a 286.

The sound does not start until the read is over, so on a slow disk you step on a pad, the game stops, and then you hear it. A sound too big for what is left of the PC's 640 KB (about 145 KB on the PS/1, which keeps DOS in its ROM; also an estimate) cannot be read into memory at all: PLAYGAME gives up and nothing plays. The extra memory above 640 KB is out of its reach.

A level loads from the same disk. Between levels the screen stays black while PLAYGAME opens and reads each file the level names (palette, map, blocks, monsters, character, sounds, and the music with a sound card); a blank file slot is not read. The game clock waits, so nothing in the level moves on. Today loads at once.

PLAYGAME reads a whole sound file into memory every time it plays it, before the game goes on. The sound then plays by itself, from the sound card. The music moves one step on every beat of the timer, and while the disk is read the timer waits too: the song stands still, the notes it was playing hum on, and afterward it goes on from where it stopped, never catching up. A sound read often (on every stroke or every shot) makes the music drag behind the game a little each time. The music's own notes cost about one percent of the PC, even in a busy song.

Tips

  • Keep sounds short. Keep a sound under 12 KB, and always under 64 KB.
  • Keep a few monsters on a screen. Ten or fewer is safe on every machine.
  • Keep moving blocks to where they count. A few animated blocks cost little, a screenful costs a lot.
  • Do not put a long sound on a block you can stand on: it plays again on every tick you touch it (see Sounds and Music).
  • Use block timers for timing, not how far the hero walks: timers are exact on a slow computer and walking is not.

pages.head: What it cannot do
pages.html:
What it cannot do

A DOS game has no way to change the speed of its own computer, so the speed is set by the player, not by the game. That means it only shows up in a player that has the Run like a menu (the web player does). The desk's PC has its own Turbo button for the same reason. The numbers are estimates, so a real 286 may feel a bit different. The menu also does not slow the music or change how a game draws, and a game that scrolls a lot will lose more on a slow machine than these rooms show.

pages.head: Make it yours
pages.html:
Make it yours

Try one change at a time, and play after each on 286:

  • Open slowpc.snd and give the long pad's slot a shorter sound, or put LONGSND in the score slot too.
  • In the Map editor, delete monsters from the crowd until the 286 keeps up.
  • In three.bbl, make the sky's time 4 ticks. The drift is slower and the game costs less.
  • Place a sound pad on a block you stand on, and hear it chop.

The home page's Starters tab has more small games like this one.
